**Subject: Electrical & electromechanical actuation for aerospace and defense (new-build + retrofit) — competitor focus Moog, Safran, Honeywell | Evidence base: Tier 2 public sources only, no user data supplied | Window: Sept 2021 – Sept 2026 | Compiled 4 Sept 2026**

## Governing Insight

**Situation.** Aircraft actuation is a supplier-concentrated, program-locked market — five firms (Moog, Safran, Parker Hannifin, Honeywell, Liebherr) are credited with 47.6% of aircraft EMA revenue, and hydraulic technology still held 44.9% of total actuator revenue in 2025 (Sources: Global Market Insights, gminsights.com/industry-analysis/electromechanical-actuators-in-aircraft-market, Jul 2026; Mordor Intelligence, mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/aircraft-actuators-market, Jul 2026).

**Complication.** On a single day — 21 July 2025 — the supply structure changed: Safran closed its $1.8bn acquisition of Collins Aerospace's flight control and actuation business (~$1.55bn 2024 revenue, 180 platforms) while being required by US regulators to simultaneously divest its own North American EMA business (~$65m 2024 sales) to Woodward (Source: Safran press release, safran-group.com, 21 Jul 2025). Yet in the same window, named engineering leaders at Triumph and Honeywell state that traditional customers are not pulling electromechanical actuation.

**Question.** Over the next several years, is electric/electromechanical actuation primarily a *demand conversion* event — hydraulics being displaced on the volume platforms — or primarily a *supply consolidation* event?

**Answer.** On the evidence available, this window has been consolidation, not conversion. EMA is gaining where it is being designed in new — missiles, space thrust-vector control, electric brakes, high-lift, AAM — while primary flight control and landing gear on the high-volume platforms remain hydraulic or are trending toward *hybrid* electro-hydraulic architectures. Near-term actuation revenue is being set by aircraft build rates, defense replenishment and supply-chain constraint, not by hydraulic-to-electric substitution.

## Market size — what is published, and what the hard anchors imply

**OBSERVATION (High).** Published sizing for nominally identical scopes disagrees by up to ~4×: "EMA in aircraft" is put at $0.58bn for 2025 (Source: MarketsandMarkets, marketsandmarkets.com/PressReleases/aircraft-electromechanical-actuators.asp, 20 Jun 2025), $2.2bn for 2025 (Global Market Insights, Jul 2026), and $2.70bn for 2025 in an A&D-led EMA scope (Fortune Business Insights, fortunebusinessinsights.com/electromechanical-actuators-market-117857, Jun 2026). Total aircraft actuators ranges $10.66bn (Mordor, Jul 2026) to $24.4bn (Fortune BI). *So what: any revenue model anchored to a single published figure inherits a 4× definitional error before a single assumption is made.*

**Triangulated internal estimate — aircraft EMA, 2025: ~$2.1bn (Low-Medium confidence).** Bottom-up, share-anchored:

| Step | Input | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Safran's divested North American EMA unit | $65m (2024 sales) | FACT — Safran PR, 21 Jul 2025 (High) |
| 2 | Safran global aircraft EMA revenue ≥ 3× the NA carve-out | ≈$195m | **ASSUMPTION** — unsourced; Safran retains European EMA/high-lift/HSTA capability (Safran product pages) |
| 3 | Five named leaders comparable within ~2× of each other | ≈$1.0bn combined | **ASSUMPTION** — unsourced; no vendor publishes individual EMA share |
| 4 | Top-5 hold 47.6% of aircraft EMA market | $1.0bn ÷ 0.476 | FACT (published) — GMI, Jul 2026 (Medium) |
| 5 | **Implied market** | **≈$2.1bn (2025)** | Derived |
| — | Sanity ceiling: hydraulic = 44.9% of a $10.66bn actuator market, and is the largest single category, so E/EM must be <$4.8bn | <$4.8bn | Mordor, Jul 2026 (Medium) |

**Reconciliation.** The internal estimate sits just below GMI ($2.2bn) and Fortune ($2.70bn), inside the ceiling implied by Mordor's technology split, and ~3.6× above MarketsandMarkets — because a $0.58bn total market would imply the five named leaders share only ~$276m between them, i.e. ~$55m each, when one *regional carve-out* of one of them transacted at $65m of sales. *So what: the MarketsandMarkets figure is best read as a narrow component-level definition, and plans built on it will understate reachable revenue by roughly 3–4×.*

## Competitive activity

**FACT (High).** Safran's acquired actuation business contributed €618m over five months of 2025 (annualising ≈€1.48bn) and *reduced* Equipment & Defense operating margin by ~40bps — segment margin rose 50bps, or 90bps excluding actuation (Source: Safran FY2025 results, safran-group.com, 13 Feb 2026). *So what: the largest actuation asset traded in this window is currently dilutive to its acquirer's margin, with ~$50m of stated run-rate synergies not due until 2028.*

**FACT (High).** Honeywell Aerospace now runs at ~$18bn annualised revenue with $18.15bn backlog (+9%), but cut FY26 organic sales guidance to 4–5% from 7–9% (Source: Honeywell Aerospace Q2 2026 earnings call, Motley Fool transcript, 12 Aug 2026). *So what: demand is not the constraint at the largest of the three focus competitors; conversion of backlog is.*

**FACT (Medium-High).** Moog guides missile-program revenue to ~$275m in FY26 (>20% growth), expects prime contractors to raise rates "by multiples" on PAC and THAAD, and states those seven-year agreements are **not yet in reported backlog** (Source: Moog Q3 FY26 call coverage, Yahoo Finance, 1 Aug 2026). *So what: reported backlog currently understates committed defense actuation demand at one of the three focus competitors.*

**INTERPRETATION (Medium).** Post-deal, the equipment tier has re-formed around two scale players, with Collins and Safran no longer competing head-to-head on actuation (Source: AviationOutlook company report, 26 Apr 2026). *So what: buyer choice on flight-control actuation for next-generation single-aisle narrows, while Woodward enters as a new US-domiciled EMA participant.*

## Customer demand

**FACT (High) — the counter-narrative datapoint.** Triumph's director of engineering for fluid power and actuation: traditional commercial-transport, military fixed-wing, vertical-lift and business-jet customers "want robust, reliable, proven solutions with low development risk which favors traditional hydraulic actuation" (Source: Aviation Week, aviationweek.com/mro/emerging-technologies/new-generation-aircraft-drive-actuator-engineering-advancements, 30 Aug 2023). **Staleness flag: observation date 2023 — the oldest core demand datapoint in this brief.** *So what: the substitution assumption embedded in most published EMA growth forecasts is not corroborated by the only named customer-facing engineering voices found.*

**FACT (High).** Moog's CEO notes narrowbody growth carries "lower content value" per aircraft than widebody (Source: Moog Q4 2025 earnings call transcript, moog.com, 21 Nov 2025). *So what: the Airbus ramp toward 70–75 A320s/month converts to actuation revenue at a materially lower rate per unit than headline delivery counts suggest.*

**OBSERVATION (Medium-High).** Aftermarket is outrunning OE: Honeywell commercial aftermarket $2.03bn (+8%) vs commercial OE $679m (+6%) — roughly 3:1 in dollars (Source: Zacks/Yahoo Finance on HONA Q2 2026, Aug 2026). *So what: retrofit-adjacent installed-base revenue is the larger near-term pool at the largest focus competitor, even as new-build rates rise.*

## Macroeconomic and external forces

**FACT (High).** Honeywell's CEO states ~2% of the supply base disproportionately constrains output, blocking "hundreds of millions of dollars in potential revenue"; Safran cites raw materials, forging and casting constraints (Sources: Motley Fool, 12 Aug 2026; Yahoo Finance/Safran FY25 call, 13 Feb 2026). *So what: across two of the three focus competitors, the binding constraint on actuation revenue is supply, not order intake.*

**FACT (High/Medium).** Airbus holds a record 8,754-aircraft backlog (~10.6 years of cover) and Boeing BCA backlog rose to $567.3bn; but A350 output is capped at six/month and A220 2026 rate was cut from 14 to 12 (Sources: AirInsight, 19 Feb 2026; Forecast International, 10 Jun 2026 and 14 Jul 2026; Boeing 10-K FY2025). *So what: demand visibility is exceptional while near-term deliverable volume — the actual revenue driver — is being revised down on the higher-content widebody platforms.*

## Industry shifts

**OBSERVATION (Medium).** EMA is displacing hydraulics where it is designed in new rather than retrofitted: electric brakes (787, 800 aircraft equipped; Riyadh Air 70+ 787-9 agreement, Nov 2025), high-lift ("electromechanical technology is now the standard" — Safran), missile fin and thrust-vector control, and space TVC (Sources: The BRAKE Report, 21 Nov 2025; Safran and Moog product pages; Honeywell Assure PR, Mar 2026). Meanwhile Safran chose *electro-hydrostatic*, not electromechanical, for electric nose landing gear (Safran PR, 20 Jul 2022), and EMA motor packaging is cited as a landing-gear integration constraint (Aviation Week, 30 Aug 2023). *So what: the addressable EMA opportunity is application-shaped rather than platform-wide, and landing gear specifically is trending hybrid rather than fully electric.*

**FORECAST (Medium, vendor-attributed).** Industry consolidation is expected to continue amid vertical integration and private-equity roll-ups (Source: Aerospace Manufacturing & Design 2026 Forecast, 27 Jan 2026), and Moog's CFO states the company feels "better prepared to integrate acquisitions today" (Moog Q3 FY26 call, 3 Aug 2026). *So what: the July 2025 restructuring of the actuation supply tier may not be the last such event in the window ahead.*

## Confidence Summary

The structural spine of this report rests on **High-confidence evidence**: company press releases (Safran, Honeywell Aerospace), SEC filings (Moog 8-K, Boeing 10-K, Honeywell Form 10-12B/A), earnings-call transcripts, and one named-source trade-journal interview. Every transaction value, revenue anchor, backlog figure and guidance change cited above is drawn from these.

**Medium confidence** applies to all market-size, share and CAGR figures — all are paid-vendor research whose scope definitions are undisclosed and mutually irreconcilable, and to the post-deal structural interpretation (secondary analyst commentary).

**Low-Medium confidence** attaches to the internal $2.1bn triangulated estimate, which depends on two explicitly unsourced assumptions (Safran's global-to-North-American EMA revenue ratio; comparability across the five named leaders).

Principal knowledge gaps, unclosed after two research passes: **(a)** EMA shipset value by aircraft type; **(b)** unit price points by application; **(c)** replacement cycle / MTBUR for aerospace EMAs; **(d)** the new-build vs retrofit revenue split; **(e)** warranty terms and like-for-like performance specifications for any vendor (UNKNOWN — no public source found; this is a program-negotiated, non-catalogue market and the absence of price lists is itself a finding). Gaps (a)–(c) block a platform-rate bottom-up build, which is why the share-anchored method above was used instead. Additionally, the strongest customer-demand evidence dates from August 2023 and should be re-tested before it is relied upon further.
